subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Suraj slammed his bag down. "My friend Elizabeth was so unfair about the cricket score," he told the whole class at lunch. "Ask anyone." Two boys nodded.

Wednesday. Suraj heard a new version in the corridor: Elizabeth had cheated and refused to admit it. He had never said that. He felt strangely uneasy, but he kept quiet.

Friday. Elizabeth stood at the classroom door with red eyes. "Why are you telling everyone I cheat?" Suraj tried to explain, but the story had already grown past him, and Elizabeth walked away without waiting.

qa.q: What did Suraj say Elizabeth was unfair about?
qa.a: Suraj said Elizabeth was unfair about the cricket score.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel when he heard the new version in the corridor?
qa.a: Suraj felt uneasy, because the story had grown into something he never said and he no longer controlled it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Suraj have used, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could have spoken to Elizabeth directly about the cricket score, since talking to the person involved stops the story from spreading. He could also ask a teacher to help settle the score.

qa.q: How does the spreading story feel to Elizabeth?
qa.a: Elizabeth is hurt and angry, shown by the red eyes at the door and the question about cheating, because Elizabeth's name is now attached to something untrue.

grounding: A boy tells the class his side of the fight, the story spreads and grows, and the friend becomes angrier so the fight is harder to mend.

subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]
passage: Tejas, you want to tell the whole class what Mohan did? Listen to your Tushar Kaka first. When I was eleven, my best friend Gopal and I fought over a game of marbles. I was sure he cheated. So I told the boys in my lane. Then the boys at school. By the third day, the story was that Gopal had stolen my marbles and hit me. I had said neither! Gopal heard it from someone else, and he was so angry he wouldn't even walk down the same road as me. I wanted to be proved right; instead I lost him for a whole year. We only made up at his sister's wedding.

qa.q: What had the story become by the third day?
qa.a: That Gopal had stolen the marbles and hit him.

qa.q: Why did young Tushar tell everyone his side?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure Gopal had cheated, and wanted to be proved right.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept the friendship?
qa.a: Talking to Gopal directly about the marbles instead of telling the lane and the school; spreading the story made it grow and harder to mend.

qa.q: How did Gopal experience the story spreading?
qa.a: Gopal heard an exaggerated version from someone else and was so angry and hurt that he avoided even walking the same road for a year.

grounding: Shows a boy telling others his side of a quarrel to be proved right, and the story growing until his friend is angrier and the rift lasts.

subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]
passage: The school picnic bus was packed and noisy, and Hemant was still angry. Sharmila, the quiz captain, had picked Ravi instead of him for the inter-school team. 'She's so unfair,' he told the boy beside him. By the next stop, three rows knew. By the time they reached the dam, the story had grown: Sharmila picked only her friends; Sharmila said Hemant was stupid. Sharmila had said nothing like that. At lunch she marched up to him, eyes wet and furious. 'You told everyone I called you stupid?' Hemant opened his mouth. He hadn't said that exactly. But he had started it. She sat at the far end of the bus all the way home.

qa.q: Where was the picnic bus going?
How did Hemant feel when Sharmila confronted him?
qa.a: He was stuck for words and probably ashamed, knowing he hadn't said it exactly but had started the story.

qa.q: What could Hemant have done instead of telling the bus?
qa.a: Ask Sharmila privately why she chose Ravi, or talk to the quiz teacher; spreading his side only made the story grow and her angrier.

qa.q: What was the picnic like for Sharmila?
qa.a: Sharmila heard she'd said things she never said, so she felt hurt and furious, and sat far away all the way home.

grounding: Illustrates a boy telling classmates his friend was unfair, and the story spreading and growing until she is angrier and harder to make up with.
